title: Choose Your Entity With the Exit in Mind
summary: See how entity selection can shape growth, access to capital, and the tax implications of a future exit for Technology and Life Sciences companies.
body_markdown:
Some of the decisions that matter most at exit are made long before anyone is thinking seriously about selling the company.


Entity selection is one of them. For[technology](https://www.cbiz.com/industries/technology) and[life sciences](https://www.cbiz.com/industries/life-sciences) company founders, the structure chosen at formation becomes consequential as the business matures. By the time a transaction is taking shape, choices made years earlier may already be influencing the path forward.


A founder does not need to predict exactly how the company will exit. There is value, however, in understanding how today’s structure may behave if the company’s ambitions become reality.


## Start With the Business You Intend to Build


A useful entity discussion begins with a simple question: What kind of company are you trying to build?


For a closely held business expected to produce steady income for its owners, pass-through taxation may carry considerable appeal. A company built to pursue institutional investment faces different pressures.


For technology and life sciences companies, funding can quickly become the deciding factor. A structure that works well during the founder-funded stage may become less practical once professional investors enter the picture.


That is why entity selection should account for where the business expects its capital to come from, rather than focusing exclusively on its tax position at formation.


## Where LLCs, S Corporations, and C Corporations Fit


An **LLC** offers significant governance flexibility. When taxed as a partnership, it generally allows income and losses to pass through to owners. Those characteristics can suit businesses that expect to generate current cash flow for their owners.


The calculation changes when institutional capital becomes part of the plan. Professional investors may prefer the familiarity of a C corporation, while partnership taxation can create additional filing considerations for investors as a company’s footprint grows.


An **S corporation** also offers pass-through taxation, though with greater restrictions around ownership. Certain shareholders are ineligible, and the structure generally allows only one class of stock. Those rules can limit flexibility as the ownership base evolves.


A **C corporation** often fits more naturally into the venture ecosystem. Investors are familiar with the structure, and commonly used venture financing documents are built around it. The trade-off includes potential taxation at both the corporate and shareholder levels.


For a growth company, the analysis should extend beyond today’s tax bill. The structure has to support where the company expects to go.


## QSBS Can Put a Different Lens on the Decision


For qualifying C corporations, qualified small business stock (QSBS) under section 1202 can have a meaningful effect on the after-tax economics of an exit.


Eligible noncorporate shareholders may exclude a portion, and potentially all, of qualifying gain from federal income tax when the requirements are satisfied. Only eligible C corporations can issue QSBS.


Recent changes expanded the potential benefit for qualifying stock issued after July 4, 2025. That stock may be eligible for a 50% gain exclusion after a three-year holding period, increasing to 75% after four years and 100% after five years. An early exit leaves the taxable portion subject to a special 28% tax rate, however.


The exclusion cap also increased from $10 million to $15 million or 10 times basis, if greater. The gross-asset threshold increased from $50 million to $75 million.


Stock issued before July 4, 2025, remains subject to the previous rules, including the five-year holding period, $10 million exclusion cap, and $50 million gross-asset threshold.


These potential benefits make timing important. Waiting until a sale is approaching to investigate QSBS may mean discovering that decisions affecting eligibility were made years earlier.


## Small Ownership Decisions Can Follow You to Exit


One particularly important QSBS requirement concerns how shareholders receive their stock.


Eligible shareholders generally must acquire stock directly from a qualifying C corporation at original issuance. Suppose founders want to adjust ownership shortly after formation. Transferring existing shares between shareholders may look like a simple solution, but stock purchased from an existing shareholder generally does not satisfy the original-issuance requirement.


The implications may not surface until years later.


That makes the cap table more than an administrative record. For a company pursuing QSBS treatment, documentation showing how and when shares were issued can become important support for a future eligibility analysis.


And that analysis should continue as the company develops. QSBS includes requirements related to the corporation’s activities during the applicable period. Changes to the business can therefore warrant another look at eligibility rather than assuming a determination made years earlier still holds.


## Your Future Buyer May Care About Structure Too


Financing drives many early entity conversations. At exit, the buyer introduces another perspective.


Some buyers, particularly in private equity transactions, may value a structure that provides a step-up in the tax basis of acquired assets. That preference can affect transaction structuring and may sometimes lead to additional restructuring before a sale.


The distinction between valuation and transaction economics matters. Entity structure alone does not determine what a company is worth. But it can influence how a prospective buyer evaluates the economics of acquiring it.


Founders do not need to choose an entity around a hypothetical buyer years in advance, but they should recognize that structure can affect the options available once a real buyer appears.


## Build for Optionality


Few founders have perfect visibility into an eventual exit. The company may pursue institutional capital earlier than expected, or a strategic opportunity could change the plan entirely. Entity planning should leave room for the business to evolve.


The same applies to QSBS. Its potential benefit can be significant, but qualification depends on requirements that reach back into a company’s history. Decisions around stock issuance and documentation deserve attention well before an exit process begins.[Learn more about QSBS here](https://www.cbiz.com/services/tax/business-tax/qualified-small-business-stock) .


Thoughtful entity planning can give founders and investors more choices when those early ambitions become something tangible. We understand you may not know exactly when, or how your company will exit, but early planning can help keep more options available. After years spent building value, that flexibility matters.
